venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence

title: WISE: A lightweight, weakly-supervised model for onboard fire smoke detection and localization
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Wildfire smoke detection from satellite imagery is critical for early warning and rapid response. For onboard satellite deployment, detection systems must operate under strict memory and latency constraints while providing spatially informative outputs for downstream decision-making. Existing tile-level classification methods are computationally efficient but lack spatial localization, whereas pixel-level segmentation approaches provide detailed masks yet are typically too computationally demanding for real-time onboard execution. To address this gap, we propose WISE (Weakly-supervised Inference-efficient Smoke Extraction), a deployment-oriented framework for onboard fire smoke detection and localization. WISE leverages only tile-level annotations through a teacher–student distillation strategy, where an offline teacher provides soft spatial supervision to a lightweight WISE-Student optimized for efficient onboard inference. The student jointly predicts tile-level smoke presence and smoke probability maps within a single forward pass, enabling spatially informative detection under strict computational constraints. WISE was evaluated through in-orbit execution aboard the ISS-mounted IMAGIN-e payload. Three model variants achieve average inference times of 0.10 s, 0.14 s, and 0.26 s per tile, indicating near-real-time per-tile inference within onboard resource limits. Ground-based experiments on Landsat 5 and Landsat 8 imagery further indicate effective detection and spatially informative localization. The best-performing variant achieves a mean tile-level F1 score of 0.964 and a mean pixel-level F1 score of 0.750 across 10 runs, while containing only 0.12M parameters and requiring approximately 3 GFLOPs. Together, these results indicate that WISE is a practical candidate for low-latency wildfire smoke monitoring from space under onboard resource constraints.

title: Evolving transformers with reinforcement learning-enhanced Grey Wolf Optimisation for remote sensing image segmentation
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Semantic segmentation of remote sensing images (RSI) faces various challenges due to the presence of multi-scale objects with high intra-class and low inter-class variations. Existing models often show limited robustness in tackling diverse remote sensing benchmarks and modalities under closed-set settings. To address the above challenges, we propose a new Grey Wolf Optimisation (GWO) variant-optimised encoder architecture, a new Gaussian-enhanced self-attention strategy and a gradient-guided Convolutional Block Attention Module (GGCBAM), to adapt to different segmentation tasks under closed-set settings effectively. Specifically, informed by loss gradients, GGCBAM is able to identify channel/spatial features not only important but also critical to prediction. The new self-attention variant utilises a Gaussian distribution-based bias to better emphasise local details. Hybrid attention strategies by stacking GGCBAM and Gaussian-enhanced self-attention methods in two opposite sequential orders are constructed. The proposed GWO algorithm is used to optimise the numbers of these hybrid attention blocks and their fusion weights in the dual-branch encoder for dynamic architecture generation. This new GWO variant employs 3D geometric shapes and deep reinforcement learning algorithms, i.e. Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) and Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C), for hybrid leader construction and search action selection, respectively, to increase search diversity. As indicated in empirical studies, our optimised network effectively extracts important global spatial context while preserving vital fine-grained local structures, and outperforms a number of state-of-the-art transformer networks for solving diverse segmentation tasks.

title: A multi-sensor and multi-temporal GeoAI framework for resolving ecological scale mismatch in Antarctica
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Advances in remote sensing (RS) and artificial intelligence (AI) are enabling new approaches to ecological monitoring across spatial and temporal scales. However, vegetation mapping in polar environments remains constrained by a fundamental mismatch between the fine spatial scale of ecological processes and the coarse resolution of satellite observations, as well as by limited availability of biologically reliable training data. In this study, we address these challenges by developing an end-to-end GeoAI framework that integrates field observations, drone imagery, and satellite time-series data to enable cross-scale vegetation mapping. We propose a progressive weak-to-strong labelling workflow that begins with 1) biologically grounded quadrat annotations, to create iteratively expanded training data along with 2) spectral similarity combined with machine learning, followed by 3) training with deep learning (DL) models for pixel-level segmentation. Native Sentinel-2 observations (10–20 m spatial resolution) were processed using DL-based super-resolution to an approximately 1 m output grid. High-resolution drone DL predictions were subsequently transformed into fractional cover labels aligned to the super-resolved satellite grid, supporting cross-scale modelling across centimetre-to-metre resolutions. We evaluate multiple DL architectures using spatially separated UAV evaluation data and assess satellite-scale performance as agreement with UAV-derived fractional cover reference labels. Our results demonstrate that the proposed framework substantially improves the scalability and ecological relevance of vegetation mapping in data-limited environments. The best-performing drone-scale DL model (DeepLabv3+) achieved an overall accuracy of 0.91 and a Macro-F1 score of 0.85 for fine-scale vegetation segmentation. At the satellite scale, the U-Net fractional-cover model achieved strong predictive performance for dominant vegetation classes, including cyanobacteria (R 2 = 0.94) and red Hennediella heimii moss (R 2 = 0.88), with reduced performance for spectrally complex or sparsely represented classes, demonstrating effective cross-scale vegetation mapping despite challenges associated with sub-pixel heterogeneity and spectral mixing. This study provides a generalisable methodological framework for integrating multi-sensor data and AI in ecological RS, demonstrating strong cross-scale performance while illustrating the challenges of capturing fine-scale vegetation heterogeneity at satellite scales.

title: Extending ocean color product to three dimensions assisted by high spectral resolution lidar data
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Satellite ocean color remote sensing has revolutionized our understanding of global marine ecosystems, but remains fundamentally limited to two-dimensional (2D) observations. To address this limitation, we propose a Depth-Resolved Generalized Inherent Optical Property (DR-GIOP) model that merges passive multispectral remote sensing reflectance ( R rs ) from MODIS-Aqua with active depth-resolved particulate backscattering profiles ( b bp ) from High Spectral Resolution Lidar (HSRL). Using lidar derived b bp ( z ) at a single wavelength and ocean color sensor derived spectral R rs ( λ ) as inputs, the model solves for depth-resolved spectral non-water absorption a pg ( z , λ ), particulate backscattering b bp ( z , λ ), and chlorophyll-a concentration Chl ( z ). We validated this model using coincident MODIS, airborne HSRL, and shipborne in-situ measurements from the SABOR campaign and three NAAMES campaigns. The results demonstrate that DR-GIOP successfully reconstructs reasonable three-dimensional (3D) optical structures, achieving the correlation coefficient r =∼0.85 for a pg ( z , λ ), b bp ( z , λ ), and Chl ( z ).Comparative analysis indicates that DR-GIOP significantly outperforms traditional 2D models such as Seeded GIOP, GIOP-DC, and QAA. Furthermore, we quantitatively analyze the shallow-layer bias of passive 2D remote sensing and demonstrate how active–passive fusion effectively mitigates this bias. This study proposes a promising framework for 3D ocean color reconstruction, offering new insights for future multi-sensor satellite missions. In the future, we can envision the realization of a satellite that carries an advanced HSRL and multi-spectral sensors, providing high accuracy of b bp ( z ) and R rs ( λ ) and promising 3D ocean subsurface observations at a global scale.

title: Bridging cloud-induced gaps in MODIS leaf area index products using high-frequency geostationary satellite observations
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Leaf Area Index (LAI) is a fundamental variable for characterizing vegetation canopy structure and ecosystem functioning. However, persistent cloud contamination substantially constrains the spatiotemporal continuity of LAI products derived from polar-orbiting satellite observations. In contrast, geostationary satellites provide dense temporal sampling, offering a valuable observational basis for filling data gaps in polar-orbiting satellite products. To bridge this observational gap, this study develops an observation-complementary framework that integrates high-frequency Himawari-8 Advanced Himawari Imager (AHI) observations with MODIS LAI products to achieve LAI reconstruction in cloud-prone regions. Within this framework, AHI observations are first used to retrieve LAI at a spatial resolution of 2 km using a Random Forest model trained with a high-quality MODIS-based benchmark dataset, and are then downscaled to 500 m using MODIS-derived spatial texture information. The reconstructed AHI LAI is subsequently integrated into low-quality or missing MODIS pixels to generate a fused AHI-MODIS LAI dataset over China. Validation against in-situ measurements and cross-comparison results show that the fused product maintains reasonable numerical consistency and stable temporal trajectories. Data availability increases from 70.70% to 90.90% under the 4-day compositing cycle. These results indicate that geostationary-polar-orbiting observation complementarity provides a practical pathway for improving the continuity and usability of optical LAI products in persistently cloudy regions, while remaining subject to the constraints of optical observations and cross-scale reconstruction assumptions.

title: BD-Diff: Generative Diffusion Model for Image Deblurring on Unknown Domains with Blur-Decoupled Learning
TAME-MA: Taming Mobile Agents via Trajectory-Level Trustworthiness Under Jailbreak Manipulations
PosePAL: Efficient Animal Pose Labeling Using Point Trackers
abstract: Abstract Automatically estimating animal poses from videos is important for studying animal behavior. Existing methods do not perform reliably, partly because they rely on high-quality training data, and existing such datasets are small. It is challenging and expensive to create such data, due to the large variations in animal morphology and the difficulty of frame-wise video annotation in general. In this paper, we introduce an animal pose labeling pipeline that leverages test-time optimization of a point tracker, providing temporally-consistent annotations at low cost. Given a video, we fine-tune a lightweight appearance embedding inside a pre-trained general-purpose point tracker on a sparse set of annotated frames. These annotations can be obtained from human labelers or off-the-shelf pose detectors. The fine-tuned model is then applied to the rest of the frames for automatic labeling. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance at a reasonable annotation cost. We believe our pipeline offers a valuable tool for the automatic quantification of animal behavior. Visit our project webpage at https://zhuoyang-pan.github.io/animal-labeling .

title: Voxelized 3D Gaussian Representation for Dense Visual SLAM on Embedded Vision System
Pseudo-label Refinement and Model-State Recovery for Continual Test-Time Adaptation on Semantic Segmentation
Sampling-Free Universal Domain Adaptive Object Detection with Synergistic Optimization Alignment
abstract: Abstract Universal Domain Adaptive Object Detection (UniDAOD) addresses domain shifts in open-world scenarios without assuming pre-defined shared categories between source and target domains. Despite progress in this field, existing methods rely heavily on thresholding techniques to filter private category samples, which introduces challenges in hyperparameter tuning and handling noisy data. To overcome these limitations, we propose Synergistic Optimization Alignment (SOA), a sampling-free framework that tackles two challenges inherent in UniDAOD: multi-scale discriminator discrepancy and task-dominant gradient conflict. To address the discrepancy among multi-scale discriminators, we propose Multi-Scale Discriminator Alignment (MDA) to adaptively aggregate under-aligned discriminators for shared classes, ensuring consistent feature alignment across scales. To address task-dominant gradient conflicts, we propose Gradient Coordinated Optimization (GCO), which suppresses conflicting domain-alignment gradients and coordinates their magnitudes to prevent domain over-alignment, thereby mitigating private-class interference while preserving beneficial domain-invariant supervision. Extensive experiments on open-set, partial-set, and closed-set domain adaptation benchmarks demonstrate that SOA outperforms state-of-the-art UniDAOD and DAOD methods. Code is available at https://github.com/zyfone/SOA .

title: Nested generative downscaling of passive microwave satellite data for navigation-scale Arctic sea ice forecasting
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Rapid Arctic sea ice decline is increasing the accessibility of high-latitude shipping routes, but route-scale planning remains limited by the spatial resolution and ice-edge accuracy of Arctic sea ice concentration (SIC) forecasts. Coarse forecast products can smooth marginal ice zones, narrow straits, and fine-scale ice-edge features that are important for identifying navigable corridors during seasonal melt and freeze-up. Here we introduce IceNest, a navigation-oriented Arctic SIC forecasting framework that generates daily 6.25 km SIC forecasts up to 30 days ahead. IceNest couples a deep learning-based 25 km pan-Arctic forecast ensemble with a conditional diffusion model for residual downscaling. The forecasting ensemble uses the long OSI SAF SSM/I(S) passive microwave record together with historical environmental variables from ERA5, while the downscaling model learns AMSR-scale residual corrections from AMSR-series observations. Across 2020–2023, IceNest outperformed damped persistence and the evaluated Copernicus Climate Change Service seasonal forecast systems in terms of binary accuracy and integrated ice-edge error, with the largest gains during summer melt and autumn freeze-up. Route simulations along the Northeast Passage further yielded smaller errors in navigable-window timing and route distance than GloSea5/6 when evaluated against an AMSR2-based reference, highlighting the framework’s relevance to Arctic transit planning.

title: HELIOS-Net: Hourly daytime estimation of land surface temperature with integration of observational solar-cloud-satellite geometry and deep neural network
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Geostationary satellite-based land surface temperature (LST) is vital for monitoring diurnal thermal dynamics owing to its extensive spatial coverage and high temporal resolution. However, frequent cloud cover results in substantial data gaps, limiting its practical utility for reliable thermal monitoring applications. The solar-cloud-satellite geometry (SCSG) effect has recently been introduced to reflect direct cloud radiative effects in LST reconstruction, but its application has been largely limited to polar-orbiting satellites. To address this limitation, we propose HELIOS-Net, a deep learning (DL) framework for hourly daytime LST reconstruction using the GEO-KOMPSAT-2A satellite across South Korea, central Japan, and southeastern Australia. The framework combines SCSG-based regime partitioning with a generative adversarial network (GAN) to reconstruct spatially continuous all-sky LST by leveraging satellite observations and various meteorological and topographic variables. Validation against in-situ observations demonstrated that HELIOS-Net achieved high performance across all regions, with coefficient of determination (R 2 ) values of 0.63–0.94 and root mean square error (RMSE) values of 2.45–7.65 °C under cloudy-sky conditions. Comparative evaluation further indicated an overall performance advantage over ERA5-Land and an existing all-sky LST product derived from satellite observations. Additional analyses confirmed that both the SCSG effect and the DL framework contribute to enhancing the fidelity of hourly daytime LST reconstruction. These results highlight the potential of the proposed framework to enable high-quality, spatially continuous all-sky LST monitoring from geostationary satellites, providing a promising approach mitigating cloud-induced data gaps under diverse viewing geometries and environmental conditions.

title: PatchFusion: Resilient LiDAR-camera fusion for point cloud semantic segmentation in autonomous driving
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: LiDAR-camera fusion for point cloud semantic segmentation is essential for accurate and reliable 3D perception of autonomous driving systems. Contemporary LiDAR-camera fusion approaches predominantly integrate the pixel-level camera features located by projected points to augment the corresponding 3D points, which can be abstractly defined as point-pixel fusion strategy. Although such point-pixel fusion mode has been proved to be effective and widely used in practice, the strategy has two non-ignorable defects: (1) dependent on precise point-pixel projection correspondence, (2) limited by just using extremely little image information. Besides, the LiDAR-only inference in offline fusion fails to utilize the synchronously obtained images to achieve a dynamic fusion for 3D perception, while LiDAR-camera fusion inference in online fusion still encounters challenges of field of view (FoV) discrepancy between sensors. Moreover, the corruption robustness of LiDAR-camera fusion methods for 3D semantic segmentation, a crucial factor for the practical reliability of perception systems, has received limited attention. Thus, focusing on addressing above challenges, we develop the point-patch fusion mode, and construct PatchFusion framework as a systematic and promising solution to enhance performance and resilience of LiDAR-camera fusion perception in realistic and complex driving scenes. Specifically, in PatchFusion, we propose to leverage cross-attention mechanism to implement high-quality point-patch fusion by automatically searching what information should be highlighted or suppressed from the local patch of image, thereby alleviating the adverse effects of projection errors, maximizing the utilization of the high-density image information, and being more robust to the potential image corruptions. Besides, we integrate the strengths of offline and online fusion modes and propose a bidirectional cross-modality knowledge distillation strategy, aiming to further enhance the performance and robustness for predictions within and outside camera FoV. Finally, to bridge the research gap regarding the corruption robustness of LiDAR-camera fusion methods, we design a specialized dataset corruption suite for public multimodal datasets to simulate complex evaluation conditions by synthesizing projection noises and image corruptions. Extensive experiments on well-known datasets in autonomous driving (SemanticKITTI and nuScenes) demonstrate that PatchFusion can effectively improve the performance and resilience of LiDAR-camera fusion for 3D semantic segmentation on both clean and corrupted datasets. The relevant code will be available at https://github.com/sssssyf/PatchFusion .

title: SNAIL-Radar-Indoor:A large-scale handheld LiDAR–4D radar–IMU dataset for robust SLAM in degraded environments
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Multimodal sensing, particularly 4D imaging radar, is promising for emergency search and rescue because it remains informative under smoke and highly reflective structures. However, existing public radar datasets predominantly record outdoor vehicle motion or clean indoor spaces. We present SNAIL-Radar-Indoor, a large-scale handheld LiDAR–4D radar–IMU dataset for SLAM in smoke and other degraded environments. Extending our previous outdoor SNAIL-Radar benchmark, the new release contains 217 sequences totaling approximately 850 min, collected at 13 sites across six scene types, including offices, abandoned buildings, halls, factory workshops, underground parking areas, and connecting outdoor spaces. The sequences cover corridors, rooms, staircases, narrow corners, indoor–outdoor transitions, reflective structures, dynamic crowds, and real smoke. Data were recorded using a compact self-developed integrated platform comprising a 3D LiDAR, a low-cost single-chip 4D imaging radar, a consumer-grade IMU, and an optional barometer. Repeated traversals and closed paths are included where feasible to support place recognition and loop-closure evaluation. The released trajectories are method-generated references and do not constitute independent absolute ground truth. Smoke-free sequences mainly use loop-consistent LIO references; fully smoke-dominated sequences use an iRIOM-based radar–IMU reference with AHRS and barometer constraints; and partially degraded sequences use a smoke-aware piecewise RLIO reference. Closed sequences additionally include start–end LiDAR registration constraints, while non-closed sequences are accompanied by map-based end-to-end displacement checks. The dataset supports research on radar and multimodal registration, smoke-robust odometry and mapping, denoising, environmental perception, and navigation in degraded environments.

title: Enhanced early warning of extreme river discharge events in the Yangtze River Basin using atmospheric circulation signals
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Early warning of extreme river discharge events (ERDEs) is crucial for water resources management and disaster reduction in the Yangtze River Basin (YRB), yet substantial uncertainty remains in their prediction. This study proposes a novel strategy to enhance ERDE early warning by detecting its associated atmospheric circulation signals. We develop DetRF, a machine learning model that integrates anomaly detection with a balanced random forest ensemble. DetRF was trained and validated using ERA5 reanalysis data from 2000 to 2019 and independently applied to 2020–2024, with its early warning performance evaluated against satellite-based precipitation and reanalysis river discharge data. Across eight subregions of the YRB, DetRF effectively detects ERDE-related atmospheric circulation signals, achieving mean recall, precision, and F1 score values of 0.756, 0.506, and 0.576, respectively, and consistently outperforming benchmark machine learning models. The detected signals accurately capture key synoptic features associated with hydrological extremes, including the positions and intensities of troughs, vortices, and cyclones, as well as moisture transport. More than 99% of the detected signals are followed by precipitation within five days, while persistent precipitation occurs in over 67% of cases across both local and upstream regions. More importantly, an average of 93.8% of DetRF-detected circulation signals are followed by at least one ERDE within the subsequent five days. These findings establish a direct link between specific atmospheric circulation signals and subsequent hydrological extremes, offering a new pathway for extending ERDE early warning beyond conventional hydrological prediction. The proposed framework is particularly promising for regions where hydrological observations are sparse.

title: Estimating supraglacial lake bottom ablation rates by integrating ICESat-2 repeat track data and multi-temporal sentinel-2 imagery
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Supraglacial lakes are widely distributed across the Greenland Ice Sheet (GrIS) each summer. The resulting meltwater-enhanced ablation effect plays a critical role in understanding the GrIS surface mass balance but remains poorly quantified. Inspired by the insight that longer meltwater persistence leads to stronger meltwater-enhanced ablation, this study proposes a novel method to directly estimate supraglacial lake bottom ablation rates at centimeter-per-day scale using satellite observations. First, we map multi-temporal supraglacial lake extents from Sentinel-2 imagery to estimate cumulative meltwater-covered days. Then, we derive ablation depths at the lake bottom and surrounding bare ice by differencing ICESat-2 repeat track data acquired before and during the melt season. Next, we perform linear fitting between lake bottom ablation depths and cumulative meltwater-covered days along the ICESat-2 tracks to calculate both the lake bottom ablation rate and the bare ice ablation rate. Finally, we evaluate the magnitude of the meltwater-enhanced ablation effect. We apply this method to 26 supraglacial lakes across the GrIS and identify a positive linear relationship between lake bottom ablation depths and cumulative water-covered days (mean Pearson correlation coefficient r = 0.70 ± 0.14, p < 0.001). The fitted mean lake bottom ablation rate (4.50 ± 1.15 cm/day) significantly exceeds the mean bare ice ablation rate (1.98 ± 0.52 cm/day). Meltwater in supraglacial lakes therefore enhances ablation rate by ∼ 1.3 ± 0.5 times, with values ranging from 0.6 to 2.4, consistent with previous field measurements (1.1–1.4 times) and numerical model simulations (1.1–1.7 times). In summary, this study provides a first quantitative satellite-based estimate of meltwater-enhanced ablation across the GrIS under varying ablation intensities, and may improve our understanding of GrIS surface melt process.

title: Analysis of intraday urban thermal anisotropy and downward shortwave radiation through UAV experiment and coupled model
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: The pronounced thermal radiation anisotropy observed in rapidly urbanizing areas arises from the complex interplay of solar downward shortwave radiation (DSWR), building geometry, and local topography. To address this, we propose a novel framework, termed GRay-AU3SM-IRT, for the analysis of urban thermal anisotropy (UTA). The study was conducted in a representative mountainous city in Chongqing, China. A specific 0.4 × 0.4 km 2 area, characterized by buildings and terrain on 10° slopes, was selected for analysis at hourly resolution. The simulations showed strong agreement with measured data, achieving a root mean square error below 0.46 K and a coefficient of determination exceeding 0.79. The analysis reveals that UTA shows pronounced diurnal variations: it intensifies gradually in the morning, peaks at solar noon with clear hotspot formation, and generates secondary hotspots in the afternoon due to changing solar azimuth and slope effects. The morning striped distribution pattern caused by building geometry diminishes with declining solar irradiance and disappears by afternoon. Diurnal trends in the UTA Effect (UTAE), directional brightness temperature (DBT), DBT Effect (DBTE), and DSWR are generally aligned. Notably, UTAE and DBTE peak before DSWR, while both maximum and minimum DBT peak later. The proposed framework offers key advantages: precise multi-lap UAV navigation, minimized motion artifacts, consistent temporal sampling via adaptive velocity control, gap-filling through simulation, and spatio-temporal outlier correction. It provides critical data for angle normalization and correction across diverse urban environments.

title: Remote-sensing-assisted and in situ-constrained reconstruction of 4-hourly chlorophyll-a dynamics in inland lakes using vision Mamba and temporal attention
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Chlorophyll a (Chl-a) is widely used to indicate eutrophication and bloom risk in inland waters, but daily Sentinel-3 observations alone cannot resolve transient sub-daily variability represented in partially observed 4-hourly in situ Chl-a records. This study therefore develops VGTA (Vision Mamba–GKOA–TCN-Attention), a staged remote-sensing-assisted and in situ-constrained framework that integrates daily Sentinel-3 OLCI-derived priors with partially observed 4-hourly in situ Chl-a sequences and binary observation masks. A 20-dimensional OLCI-derived feature space provides spectral–spatial priors for Chl-a estimation and bloom-risk state identification. GKOA optimizes TCN-Attention to reconstruct masked values within partially observed 4-hourly in situ Chl-a sequences. Vision Mamba outperformed CNN– and Transformer-based models in Chl-a estimation, achieving 94.8% accuracy, a Macro-F1 score of 0.909, and a Bloom-F1 score of 0.870. Ablation experiments confirmed the contributions of bidirectional contextual modeling, positional embedding, selective state-space modeling, and gating. Under Missing Completely at Random, block-missing, and real missing scenarios, GTA improved reconstruction performance by 12.71–55.54% relative to the best baseline models. Uncertainty increased once continuous gaps reached seven days, defining a practical boundary of data-driven reconstruction. Chl-a fluctuations and bloom-risk transitions can unfold within a day, and daily satellite snapshots may blur their timing or miss short events. Reconstruction of masked time steps within partially observed 4-hourly in situ Chl-a sequences can support earlier identification of bloom-risk transitions, more timely field sampling and management responses, and temporally finer monitoring of inland waters.

title: Reference-anchored envelope modelling for predicting tree mortality hotspots driven by drought
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Predicting tree mortality hotspots driven by drought remains challenging, since vulnerability to drought is strongly influenced by climate, landform, and substrate. We propose a novel reference-anchored, quantile-envelope susceptibility model-implemented through a reproducible workflow- that exports mortality-resemblance (high-risk) environments from three confirmed tree-mortality footprints (training AOIs), based on semi-arid conifer and evergreen sclerophyllous forests in Cyprus, to produce wide screening layers. The approach combines (i) physiographic similarity derived from AOI-calibrated envelopes for slope, multi-scale topographic position and curvature (broad quantiles; majority-rule), (ii) exposure constraints via circular aspect windows, warm-season solar loading (April-September) and substrate (lithology) filtering, (iii) a drought severity gate (SPEI-12 (Standardized Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index-12) ≤ -1.4), and (iv) Landsat event-year spectral collapse relative to a fixed 3-year pre-event baseline, coupled with a year + 1 persistence rule to suppress transient stress. Our within-AOI evaluation (forest-only) showed substantial representativeness (coverage 70.49–85.35%), while recovering most reference mortality pixels (recall 67.62–100%). In 2025, two independent mortality sites were identified in Cyprus, coinciding with exceptional drought (SPEI < -2) and a sharp decline in the Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR) consistent with foliage browning, and occurring within high-risk zones as mapped in the final risk map. As a plausibility check, both 2025 sites fell within pre-mapped high-risk zones, with 83.50% and 82.69% of their forested area exceeding HEAT ≥ 0.60 and mean risk scores of 84.91% and 75.55%, respectively. With 18.88% of Cyprus’s total forest flagged as high-risk, the probability of this co-occurrence being random is p ≈ 0.036 (binomial test). Anchoring calibration to local mortality footprints makes the approach readily transferable to other regions with documented events.

title: A Targeted–Refined Framework for wind turbine detection integrating AlphaEarth Foundations and high-resolution multispectral satellite imagery
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: The rapid expansion of clean energy systems, particularly wind and solar power, has made large-scale monitoring of related infrastructure using high-resolution multispectral satellite imagery increasingly important yet challenging. Conventional wind turbine detection approaches rely on pixel-level analysis of high-resolution imagery or sliding-window strategies. These methods often suffer from computational redundancy, low efficiency, and high false-positive rates, making them inadequate for supporting large-area surveys and operational monitoring. To address these limitations, this study proposes a Targeted–Refined framework based on AlphaEarth Foundations. First, a wind turbine sample database was constructed for model training and evaluation in Tianjin. In the Targeted Candidate Screening stage, a lightweight multi-layer perceptron classifier exploits the geospatial representations provided by AEF, enabling rapid identification of candidate regions while reducing the search space to approximately 5% of the original image patches. In the Refined Detection stage, high-resolution Jilin-1 satellite imagery is incorporated, and a YOLO model performs precise detection within the candidate regions. Experimental results show that the proposed framework achieves a recall of 96.85%, a precision of 98.41%, and an F1-score of 97.63% on the Tianjin test set. Furthermore, the trained model is directly applied to the plains of the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region (excluding Tianjin) for cross-regional evaluation, where it identifies 1,580 wind turbines with an F1-score of 91.33%, demonstrating strong generalization capability. Overall, this framework provides an efficient and scalable solution for detecting large-scale, spatially sparse objects, and offers a practical approach for infrastructure inventory and monitoring of wind farms and similar assets.

title: Multi-angular assessment of early-season defoliation: Evaluating the sensitivity of vegetation indices to NPV visibility in temperate broadleaved forests
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Early-season forest decline in temperate broadleaved stands often lacks detectable biochemical stress signals, manifesting primarily through reduced foliage density and increased visibility of non-photosynthetic vegetation (NPV). This study investigated the spectral separability of green leaves and NPV components under varying levels of canopy defoliation. Using a crane platform, we collected in situ leaf- and canopy-level spectrometer measurements alongside co-aligned photography to quantify the visible fraction of NPV. We analyzed the multi-angular reflectance characteristics and evaluated 35 vegetation indices (VIs) —including green biomass metrics and specialized NPV indices —using Random Forest to identify optimal spectral and geometric configurations. Sunlit young foliage exhibited high forward scatter, creating a nadir reflectance minimum. At canopy level, a nadir minimum was driven by the gap distribution resulting from sustainable forest management practices. Consequently, the optimal viewing angle for top-ranking VIs (e.g., SNC BAO , Ctr 2 , mNDVI 705 ) was near the hotspot geometry, minimizing shadowing and forest floor interference. While the total visible fraction of NPV remained mostly insensitive to viewing angles, its shaded proportion varied. VIs targeting green vegetation via red-edge and NIR domains consistently outperformed dedicated NPV indices based on SWIR cellulose and lignin absorption. This is attributed to low upper-canopy SWIR transmittance, which obscured the signals of the largely shaded NPV fraction. Top-performing VIs achieved R 2 = 0.92 for NPV visibility prediction, improving by 21 % over the best SWIR indices and 11 % over the nadir view. To accurately detect initial defoliation and overcome forest floor interference, adopting off-nadir viewing geometries is advantageous for capturing the optimal signal.

title: Unsupervised soft-min fusion of multi-sensor turbidity products using Gaussian mixture models
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Turbidity is a key indicator of water quality and particulate dynamics, making its accurate monitoring essential for aquatic ecosystem management. While satellite remote sensing enables large-scale turbidity observation, products derived from different sensors often exhibit inconsistencies due to differences in spectral responses, residual atmospheric effects, and viewing geometries. Effectively integrating such multi-source data in the absence of ground truth remains a significant challenge. Here, we propose Gaussian mixture model-based soft-min (GMMS), a fully unsupervised fusion framework in which neither model construction nor weight estimation relies on ground-truth turbidity observations. GMMS integrates Gaussian mixture modeling with a soft-min weighting strategy to identify latent error-structure contexts and adaptively assign sensor weights according to relative residual stability. By exploiting inter-sensor error characteristics, the framework enables context-aware data fusion. At the overall scale, GMMS significantly outperforms triple collocation (TC) and extended triple collocation for maximized correlation (ETCC) ( p < 0.05). Compared with in situ turbidity observations, GMMS increases the correlation coefficient from 0.798 to 0.841 and reduces the RMSE from 16.849 to 15.921 TU. Site-level evaluations further indicate enhanced robustness and reduced performance variability across monitoring stations. Simulation experiments confirm that GMMS achieves the greatest and most stable performance gains under conditions of moderate-to-high error-structure separability. Overall, GMMS provides an interpretable and transferable unsupervised fusion framework for improving multi-source satellite-derived turbidity estimates in complex riverine environments.

title: De-biasing Skeleton-Based Action Recognition with Convex Hull Adaptive Shift
IterRF: Iterative and Interpretable Mutual Enhancement for Joint Multi-Modal Image Registration and Fusion

Dual-Edged Homogeneous-Modality Similarity: Towards Visible-Infrared Modality-Incomplete Person Re-Identification with Modality Adaptive Matching
A source–medium–receiver framework for modeling wind-driven vegetation cooling in urban landscapes
abstract: Vegetation cooling in cities is often represented as a local, isotropic effect, although atmospheric processes can redistribute cooling beyond individual vegetation patches. This simplification may overlook the nonlocal and directionally structured nature of cooling propagation. We developed a physics-guided source–medium–receiver (SMR) framework for the Greater Bay Area of China to compare multi-source isotropic connectivity with prevailing-wind-conditioned connectivity. Vegetation-source strength was represented by the VCSI, and parameters estimated from 2021 to 2023 were frozen for an independent 2024 holdout and contrasting monsoon assessments. Cooling connectivity was modeled using a spatially varying distance-decay function, controlled by the wind speed, moisture content, surface albedo, terrain, and directional constraints from prevailing winds. In 2024, isotropic connectivity showed a stronger relationship with LST (r = −0.8069) than wind-conditioned connectivity (r = −0.7780) and local VCSI (r = −0.7757), with the same general ordering across monsoon and built-up receiver assessments. The source-level decay lengths ranged from 0.504 to 0.518 km, whereas the wind-conditioned emergent multi-source persistence increased from 4.13 to 4.88 km, reflecting cumulative field behaviors. Wind-relative decomposition further showed that annual connectivity was distributed across downwind, crosswind, and upwind pathways. These findings indicate that regional vegetation cooling is primarily characterized by distance-mediated, multi-source connectivity, while prevailing-wind direction acts as a scale- and condition-dependent modifier. This shift in perspective provides a physically grounded framework for effective urban climate analysis and precision greening strategies.

title: Reliable Sar oil-spill segmentation for marine monitoring Via self-supervised denoising and lightweight wavelet–state-space modeling
abstract: Reliable SAR oil-spill segmentation must simultaneously address image degradation caused by speckle and semantic confusion caused by look-alike dark features, such as low-wind areas, biofilms, and oceanic internal waves. To this end, this paper proposes the OS-AdaAttReNet-WSSNet framework, which decomposes the task into two complementary stages: self-supervised image restoration and supervised oil-spill segmentation. In the first stage, a self-supervised denoising network, AdaAttReNet, is constructed. Without requiring clean reference images, it integrates rotation-equivariant features, channel-spatial attention, and adaptive residual reconstruction to alleviate the effects of speckle on image texture, weak boundaries, and elongated structures. In the second stage, a lightweight wavelet-state-space segmentation network family, WSSNet, is developed. Multi-Scale Split Attention (MSSAtt), the Dynamic Enhanced Residual Wavelet Encoder (DE-RWE), and the Mamba-Enhanced Multi-scale Context Aggregation Upsampler (MEMCAU) are employed for multi-scale feature enhancement, wavelet-domain structural encoding, and long-range contextual fusion, respectively, thereby improving the recognition and boundary localization of irregular oil slicks. On the PALSAR and Sentinel subsets of the SOS dataset, the proposed framework achieves comparable or higher average segmentation performance than recent oil-spill-specific segmentation models. In particular, WSSNet-Tiny, with only 0.27 M parameters, substantially reduces model size and computational cost while maintaining competitive segmentation performance, demonstrating a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. In addition, experiments on six external data subsets show that the WSSNet series exhibits a certain degree of direct transferability without using target-domain data for training or adaptation. The proposed framework provides a solution for reliable and efficient SAR oil-spill monitoring that balances segmentation accuracy, computational efficiency, and transferability.

title: Global daily joint reconstruction of TROPOMI tropospheric NO 2 columns and averaging kernels with temporally aware deep learning
abstract: Achieving spatiotemporal consistency in comparisons between satellite tropospheric nitrogen dioxide (NO2) retrievals and numerical models or profile-resolving observations depends on the availability of both seamless NO2 vertical columns and their corresponding averaging kernels (AKs). However, cloud cover, aerosols, and solar-zenith-angle constraints frequently invalidate TROPOMI retrievals. Because existing reconstruction studies typically provide NO2 columns in isolation, AK-weighted analyses remain restricted to the original, fragmented observation footprints. Here we develop a temporally aware deep learning framework that jointly reconstructs TROPOMI tropospheric NO2 columns and 34-layer AKs over global land at 0.05° daily resolution from May 2018 to December 2024, with the resulting gap-filled field representing a clear-view, retrieval-consistent column and providing a lower-bound representation under persistent cloud. Because static-feature ML baselines do not explicitly represent photochemical-lifetime, boundary-layer, and transport processes, we introduce a CNN-Temporal-Attention architecture that explicitly encodes 24-hour pre-overpass meteorological dependencies. For AK, a retrieval-specific operator that lacks Vertical Column Density (VCD)-equivalent spatial priors, we exploit inter-layer continuity in vertical sensitivity through a layer-preserving 1D-CNN. Both models achieve ΔR2 ≤ 0.02 across random, temporal, and spatial-block cross-validation, with the AK model reaching a pooled R2 of 0.96; attribution patterns are consistent with the seasonal variation of the NOx photochemical lifetime, and the learned temporal weighting is consistent with cross-day boundary-layer memory, a bimodal boundary-layer cycling, and a ~2-hour upwind transport-related temporal association. Independent validation against 141 Pandora and 29 MAX-DOAS stations supports daily-to-annual accuracy, while AK-smoothed MAX-DOAS and aircraft spiral-profile comparisons support reconstructed AK physical consistency. Reconstructed fields preserve emission-control trends, COVID-19 responses, and biomass-burning signals. Co-delivering VCDs, layer-resolved AKs, and per-pixel uncertainties enables rigorous AK-weighted analysis beyond the original TROPOMI footprint.

title: High-resolution land cover mapping from coarse labels via a noisy label learning-guided cross-scale framework
abstract: High-resolution remote sensing images (HRSIs) provide essential data support for land cover mapping, where deep learning has shown great promise. However, deep learning-based methods rely on abundant high-quality annotations, while low-resolution coarse labels are difficult to use directly in HRSIs training. In this paper, a novel noisy label learning-guided cross-scale framework (NL-CSF) is proposed, which is designed to achieve high-resolution land cover mapping from coarse labels. First, a spectral-based label mask filtering strategy is developed to preliminarily optimize coarse labels. Then, an adaptive noise evaluation scheme is introduced that assigns loss weights based on the noise differences between image and label patches in the training set. Finally, we design a cross-scale transfer Transformer (CSTT) model based on the vision Transformer (ViT) architecture, and the training process is guided by a noise-weighted loss function. Two cross-scale datasets are utilized to evaluate the performance of NL-CSF in multiple spatial scale differences (10 m to 3 m, 3 m to 0.5 m, and 10 m to 0.5 m). Experimental results demonstrate that NL-CSF improves overall accuracy (OA) by at least 7%, 6%, and 4% across the three cross-scale tasks in the first dataset, and by at least 2%, 9%, and 4% in the second dataset, respectively, compared with existing methods. Furthermore, the proposed framework is applied to cross-scale mapping across Jianye District of Nanjing (urban), Sheyang County of Yancheng (agricultural), and the Yellow River Delta of Dongying (wetland), leveraging a low-resolution land cover product and high-resolution PlanetScope images to generate more precise land cover maps. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in mitigating the impact of noisy coarse labels and generating reliable high-resolution land cover maps.

title: Audio-visual fusion for near-surface wind speed estimation using surveillance cameras
abstract: Surveillance camera-based wind speed (WS) estimation provides a promising and cost-effective solution for near-surface wind sensing; however, its performance remains limited in complex urban environments due to the instability and insufficient accuracy of single-modality observations. This study proposes a surveillance audio-visual fusion framework for WS estimation, termed VA-WindNet. VA-WindNet jointly exploits wind-induced visual motion features and acoustic spectral signatures by integrating convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for spatial feature extraction with temporal neural networks for sequential modeling, together with a sequential bidirectional cross-modal interaction mechanism that progressively refines the visual and acoustic temporal representations before feature aggregation. A multi-scene audio-visual wind dataset of approximately 64 hours was constructed, and 48 VA-WindNet variants were developed by combining multiple CNN backbones with different temporal modeling modules for systematic training and evaluation. Results from real-world experiments show that the VA-WindNet model configured with DenseNet169 and a recurrent neural network achieved the best performance with an RMSE of 1.42 m/s. This corresponds to RMSE reductions of approximately 12.9% and 27.2% compared with the best video-only and audio-only configurations, respectively, and approximately 19% compared with two advanced vision-based wind speed estimation models. Under audio- and video-interference conditions, the median RMSEs of VA-WindNet variants were 1.68 m/s and 2.11 m/s, representing reductions of 33.3% and 19.5% relative to the audio-only and video-only baselines, respectively. These results highlight the potential of surveillance camera networks as a low-cost and infrastructure-efficient solution for high-resolution near-surface wind sensing in urban environments, supporting sustainable urban environmental monitoring, fine-scale wind field analysis, and smart-city-oriented observation enhancement as a complement to existing networks.

title: Shifting pathways of post-earthquake vegetation structural and functional recovery under varying earthquake disturbance intensities
abstract: Extreme disturbances (e.g. earthquakes) alter ecosystem structure and function, and shape the patterns of ecosystem resilience and carbon sink recovery. Spatial heterogeneities in varying seismic intensities may drive divergent structural and functional recovery trajectories, yet the synchrony between the two recoveries remains unclear. Moreover, the inadequate evaluation of satellite-derived biophysical products, along with the effects of climate change and human activities, may bias the interpretation of earthquake-induced vegetation recovery trajectories. Taking the 2017 Jiuzhaigou earthquake as a case study, we developed the dual-dimensional recovery assessment framework that integrated the leaf area index (LAI, proxy of structure) and gross primary productivity (GPP, proxy of function). The multiple GPP and LAI products were separately evaluated using eddy covariance observations and high-resolution reference data to select the representative vegetation structure and function proxies. The vegetation damaged areas (VDA) were then extracted using joint GPP–LAI thresholds. Subsequently, the residual analysis was served isolate the effects of climate change and human activities, as well as to quantify the impacts of earthquake disturbances on vegetation recovery during 2018–2023. The results indicated that PML-V2 GPP and MODIS LAI exhibited relatively high stability, and 56.52% of the area experienced concurrent structural and functional damage, with the earthquake disturbance contributing approximately 75% to the VDA. Early post-earthquake structural and functional recovery showed pronounced asynchrony but gradually became coordinated over time. Distinct recovery pathways of vegetation structure and function were observed across disturbance intensity zones. Specifically, in severely disturbed zones, the GPP recovered faster than LAI, which implied that functional recovery outpaced structural recovery (i.e. the function-leading recovery pathway). In contrast, the opposite pattern was observed in the moderately and weakly disturbed zones, where structural recovery preceded functional recovery (i.e. the structure-dominated pathway). The variation in leaf photosynthetic efficiency partly explained the divergent recovery dynamics between LAI and GPP under different earthquake disturbance intensities. By 2023, more than half of the area remained degraded or in ongoing recovery, which highlighted the long-term and spatially heterogeneous nature of ecosystem recovery. Our study reveals distinct post-earthquake vegetation recovery pathways from an integrated structure–function perspective. These findings provide important insights into the spatiotemporal dynamics of vegetation recovery and its implications for regional carbon cycling.

title: MambaMPD: a mamba-driven segmentation framework for marine pollution detection from remote sensing imagery
abstract: Accurate detection of marine pollution is essential for protecting coastal ecosystems and marine biodiversity. Recently, vision Mamba-based approaches have shown promise in remote sensing semantic segmentation due to their ability to efficiently capture long-range dependencies and global context. However, their potential remains largely unexplored in the context of marine pollution detection (MPD), with distinct challenges, including low signal-to-noise ratios, spatial fragmentation of pollution patterns, and indistinct boundaries caused by strong visual similarity between pollutants and the surrounding marine environment. To address these challenges, we propose MambaMPD, an enhanced Mamba-based framework tailored for marine pollution detection. MambaMPD incorporates two targeted modules that enhance the Mamba encoder with complementary structural priors: the frequency-aware augmentation (FAA) module and the multi-scale edge-guided attention (EGA) module. The FAA module strengthens the encoding process by integrating Wavelet Transforms, which decompose features into multi-scale frequency subbands. This enables the model to efficiently capture both low-frequency contextual semantics and high-frequency structural details, essential for identifying small, low-contrast, and irregular pollution patterns. Meanwhile, the EGA module adaptively integrates hierarchical Laplacian-derived multi-scale boundary cues into deep semantic representations, guiding the refinement of encoder features before decoding, thereby sharpening boundary delineation and alleviating ambiguity in visually confusing and spatially fragmented marine scenes. Additionally, a U-Net-style decoder equipped with squeeze-and-excitation attention and deep supervision is employed to progressively recover and refine semantic and spatial features across multiple scales. Extensive experiments on two benchmark marine pollution detection datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the compared methods in mIoU while maintaining significantly lower computational cost than foundation-model-based approaches. On MADOS, it surpasses OSDMamba by 3.6% in F1, and on M4D it improves Oil Spill IoU by 6.82% over TransOilSeg. The source code of our approach will be available at https://github.com/Multimodal-Intelligence-Lab-MIL/MambaMPD.

title: A Class of C 2 Point-Normal Subdivision Surfaces and Their Exact Evaluation at Arbitrary Parameters
abstract: This paper proposes techniques to construct and evaluate C 2 subdivision surfaces under control of quadrilateral meshes with unit normal vectors at the vertices. An improved C 2 modification of the Catmull-Clark subdivision scheme is first given by tuning the eigenvalues of subdivision matrices. Just like the existing C 2 modified Catmull-Clark subdivision, the improved scheme can also generate C 2 subdivision surfaces with vanishing curvature at the extraordinary points, but the flat regions near the extraordinary points have been significantly reduced. By independently applying the new modified subdivision scheme to control points and control normals of the control meshes, a class of C 2 point-normal (PN) subdivision surfaces is defined by updating the limit positions of subdivided points along the limit vectors of subdivided normals. Unlike their linear counterparts, PN subdivision surfaces can approximate control points with even higher-order accuracy while spheres and circular cylinders can be reproduced exactly. The curvatures at the extraordinary points of C 2 PN subdivision surfaces are generally non-vanishing, unless the surfaces reduce to linear subdivision surfaces. Like the classical Catmull-Clark subdivision surfaces, the C 2 modified Catmull-Clark subdivision surfaces and the C 2 PN Catmull-Clark subdivision surfaces can be evaluated exactly at arbitrary parameters. Numerical examples also demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed techniques for modeling and evaluating curvature-continuous subdivision surfaces.

title: Nonlinear responses of net ecosystem productivity to heatwaves over the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau: insights from climate and vegetation
abstract: Global climate warming has intensified heatwave disasters over the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau (QTP), exerting persistent and far-reaching impacts on the regional carbon cycle, which has attracted extensive attention from the scientific community. However, the spatiotemporal variation patterns of heatwaves over the QTP and their impacts on net ecosystem productivity (NEP) remain unclear. In this study, three heatwave indices – heatwave magnitude index (HWMI), heatwave days (HWD), and heatwave frequency (HWF) – were constructed to develop a three-level analytical framework across interannual, climatic, and vegetation dimensions. This framework was used to investigate the spatiotemporal characteristics of heatwaves over the QTP from 2003 to 2022 and their effects on the NEP. The results show that (1) heatwaves over the QTP exhibit an overall increasing trend with interannual fluctuations, with semi-arid meadow and steppe ecosystems in the southwestern QTP identified as core regions of heatwave intensification. However, QTP ecosystems appear to maintain relatively stable responses under short-duration, high-frequency heatwave disturbances. (2) The NEP over the QTP exhibited decreasing gradients from north to south and from east to west. NEP responses to heatwaves exhibited distinct spatial patterns across vegetation types, with stronger declines observed in the western arid meadow and steppe regions and the southern humid forest regions. Both extreme short-term heatwaves and prolonged heatwave events are strongly associated with NEP reductions. (3) HWMI shows a significant nonlinear negative relationship with NEP and exhibits higher sensitivity to NEP variations compared with HWD and HWF. Along climatic and vegetation gradients, the relative importance of heatwave metrics in explaining NEP variability shifts from HWMI to HWD and HWF. Therefore, attention should be paid to the potential threats of abrupt warming events to the carbon sink function of alpine ecosystems, with enhanced monitoring of abnormal high air temperatures and the implementation of heat mitigation measures. This study provides a theoretical basis and technical support for ecological conservation and disaster risk mitigation on the QTP.

title: Q-DRFormer: Query-Position Mapping Flow Prediction with Progressive Refinement for Document Rectification
abstract: Document image rectification aims to restore images degraded by geometric distortions. Existing U-shaped encoder-decoder methods rely on hierarchical upsampling operations to recover dense flow fields, which provide limited control over the displacement at individual grid positions, leading to spatial inconsistency and poor detail restoration. To address this issue, we propose Q‑DRFormer, a novel framework that formulates rectification as a set prediction task. Specifically, we design a set of queries, where each query corresponds to a position in the flow field grid and is responsible for regressing a 2D anchor point that indicates the sampling position in the distorted input. This one-to-one design establishes a deterministic query-position mapping, enabling fine-grained control and improving the spatial consistency of the predicted flow field. Exploiting this deterministic correspondence, we further propose a progressive flow refinement strategy that progressively refines anchor points through layer-wise offset prediction to enhance fine-grained restoration. Moreover, considering the lack of downstream-task-oriented evaluation in existing studies, we apply the rectification method to scene table detection and contribute a real-world test set along with corresponding evaluation metrics to fill this gap. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Q-DRFormer outperforms existing methods. The code is available at https://github.com/vvvvvair/Q-DRFormer.

title: Aboveground woody biomass regression and uncertainty estimation from spaceborne lidar and optical datasets
abstract: Woody plant encroachment continues to reshape rangeland ecosystems by altering forage availability, water balance, and carbon storage. Yet producing spatially explicit woody biomass maps that capture this fine‑scale heterogeneity remains a major challenge, particularly in regions with sparse field data. Here, we develop a cloud-based workflow that integrates the structural sensitivity of ICESat-2 canopy height measurements with the spatial continuity of multispectral imagery and environmental predictors to estimate aboveground woody biomass at 30 m resolution. To address limitations in field sampling, we derived training labels from post-fire cumulative net primary productivity (NPP), converted these values to biomass using empirical allocation factors, and trained a Random Forest model. Our approach outperforms GEDI L4A and L4B biomass products when evaluated against U.S. Forest Service FIA plots (RMSE = 5.66 vs 6.99 and 8.07 Mg/ha) and provides continuous, higher-resolution estimates across grassland, savanna, and woodland strata. While this framework enables reproducible wall-to-wall biomass mapping in data-poor regions, we emphasize that such maps may introduce spatial biases and should not be used directly for official carbon accounting without further validation. Instead, the workflow is well suited for applications requiring higher-resolution structural information, including spatial planning, habitat assessment, fuel load estimation, and local-scale fire risk modeling. These biomass surfaces may also support investigations of ecosystem functions that are tightly linked to woody cover. As new missions such as NISAR deliver L‑band SAR data sensitive to woody vegetation and soil moisture, integrating these datasets with ICESat‑2 derived datasets and optical imagery will further enhance biomass estimation and disturbance monitoring in rangeland systems.

title: Balancing solution quality and runtime in modular mobile hospital location: a hybrid approach of deep reinforcement learning and integer programming
abstract: In emergency situations such as natural disasters and infectious disease outbreaks, healthcare demand can surge rapidly and become concentrated in specific areas, and existing fixed medical facilities alone may struggle to respond to such sudden increases in demand, giving rise to the need for the rapid deployment of mobile hospitals. To address this Modular Mobile Hospital (MMH) location selection problem—which requires deriving a sufficiently high-quality solution within a limited timeframe—this study proposes a hybrid framework that integrates Integer Programming (IP) with Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). This framework leverages the strengths of both methods: the high solution quality offered by IP and the rapid solution exploration capability of DRL. Specifically, DRL is employed to screen candidate locations, after which IP determines the final locations from within this refined candidate set. Our analysis demonstrates that the proposed framework achieved up to a 93% reduction in computation time compared to IP alone, while consistently yielding improved solution quality over DRL alone across all conditions. Notably, under large-scale candidate conditions (p > 300), the framework narrowed the solution quality gap with IP to within 99.7% of IP's performance, while still producing results in a shorter amount of time. This hybrid framework offers a practical, time-efficient alternative for facility location decisions in disaster response, where rapid identification of sufficiently good solutions is essential.

title: Assessing local and transferable spectral endmembers for disturbance detection in Pinus sylvestris L. forests across Spain
abstract: Differences in forest structure, species composition, and climate across biogeographical regions challenge the reliability of spectral models for forest disturbance monitoring. This study assessed whether region-specific spectral endmembers are required to detect silvicultural interventions in Pinus sylvestris forests across Spain. Sentinel-2 spectral signatures were characterized across 18 Provenance Regions and forest development stages (young, pole, and mature stands). PRs were grouped by spectral similarity using K-means clustering, and local, transferred, and global endmember sets were incorporated into the Fusion Near Real Time (FNRT) algorithm through Linear Spectral Mixture Analysis (LMSA) and the Normalized Difference Fraction Index (NDFI). Detection performance was evaluated using 70 reference polygons representing clear-cutting and thinning intervention. Spectral analysis identified three main spectral-ecological clusters: Atlantic, Continental, and Mediterranean. Detection accuracy differed significantly among clusters, reaching 86.63 ± 15.09% in the Continental, 78.63 ± 20.87% in the Atlantic, and 70.23 ± 17.77% in the Mediterranean cluster. Silvicultural treatment also significantly affected performance, with clear-cutting achieving higher accuracy (89.60 ± 10.76%) than high- (73.02 ± 20.22%) and low-intensity thinning (72.74 ± 19.95%). In contrast, endmember origin had no significant effect on detection accuracy (p = 0.617): local endmembers achieved 80.22 ± 18.47%, compared with 78.44 ± 19.04% for global and 76.82 ± 20.22% for transferred endmembers. These results show that, despite regional spectral variability, global and transferred endmembers maintain comparable detection performance, supporting their use for large-scale operational forest monitoring while reducing the need for region-specific calibration.

title: A soil-thickness-constrained geospatial framework for reconstructing monthly shallow soil water storage across the Tibetan Plateau
abstract: Fixed-depth (FD) assumptions can substantially bias estimates of soil water storage (SWS) integrated over the 0–200 cm profile, hereafter referred to as shallow SWS, particularly in mountain regions where soil thickness (ST) varies markedly and shallow bedrock is widespread. In this study, we developed an ST-constrained framework to reconstruct monthly shallow SWS across the Tibetan Plateau (TP) at 1 km resolution over an 11-year window comprising 132 months (January 2009–December 2019) by integrating remote-sensing products, reanalysis data, and field observations. Using 1,615 in situ ST profiles and multi-source environmental covariates, we first mapped ST with a random forest model and then downscaled GLDAS soil moisture (SM) for four standard layers: 0–10, 10–40, 40–100, and 100–200 cm. Pixel-level SWS was estimated by truncating the vertical SM profile at the predicted ST, thereby preventing water from being allocated below the soil–bedrock interface. In spatial cross-validation, the ST model showed moderate spatial transferability (R 2 = 0.46, CCC = 0.62, and ubRMSE = 41.78 cm). Downscaled SM in the 0–100 cm profile was evaluated against Tibet-Obs measurements for the three upper layers. Station-based temporal Pearson’s R (mean R 2; CCC) values were 0.56 (0.40; 0.23), 0.28 (0.24; 0.06), and 0.28 (0.16; 0.02) for the 0–10, 10–40, and 40–100 cm layers, respectively. The corresponding ubRMSE (bias) values were 0.15 (−0.03), 0.12 (+0.04), and 0.15 (+0.03) m3/m3, respectively. Point-scale performance was comparatively stronger in the surface layer but weak in the 40–100 cm layer (R = 0.28; CCC = 0.02); therefore, layer-resolved SWS estimates in deep-soil regions should be interpreted cautiously as predictor-conditioned downscaled reanalysis rather than as fully in situ-validated estimates. Direct validation of the 100–200 cm layer was not feasible because in situ observations below 80 cm were unavailable; therefore, this layer should be interpreted as a profile-consistent reconstruction rather than a directly validated product. Because 81.30% of the estimated difference between the FD and ST-constrained approaches originated from the reconstructed 100–200 cm layer, the absolute magnitude of the reported storage difference and trend reduction should be interpreted with caution, although the direction of the structural bias was consistent across GLDAS and ERA5-Land. The ST-constrained SWS averaged 504.06 km3, whereas the conventional FD approach yielded 1,255.85 km3. Thus, ignoring soil–bedrock constraints caused an overestimate of 751.79 km3 (149.15%). Sensitivity analysis further showed that FD-based SWS increased nearly linearly with assumed profile depth, whereas ST-constrained estimates stabilized once the physically available storage capacity was reached. The reconstructed dataset captured a pronounced seasonal cycle and a significant wetting trend. Specifically, the ST-constrained framework indicated a moderate increase of 4.99 km3 yr−1 during 2009–2019, compared with 10.78 km3 yr−1 under the FD assumption. These findings show the importance of incorporating ST as a spatially explicit lower boundary when reconstructing shallow subsurface water storage in topographically heterogeneous mountain regions.

title: Toward a Causally-Inspired Evolving World Model for Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) has emerged as a pivotal challenge in Embodied AI, requiring an agent to navigate 3D spaces guided by natural language instructions. Drawing inspiration from human cognition, world models provide a powerful paradigm by predicting environment dynamics and enabling reasoning beyond immediate observations. However, existing world model-based VLN methods remain static once trained - their representations rely on fixed correlation-based priors rather than adaptive causal structures, making them unable to accommodate evolving confounders and changing observation-action dependencies across environments. This rigidity leads to overfitting to training-specific patterns and degraded performance under distribution shifts. To address this limitation, we propose a causally-inspired evolving world modeling framework that formulates VLN-CE as a sequence of causal partially observable Markov decision processes. Our model learns unified latent states that integrate vision, language, and action, while addressing spurious correlations through a dual-level intervention mechanism: at the observation level, frequency-domain perturbations simulate superficial appearance variations to enhance perceptual robustness; at the representation level, cross-episode confounder buffers perform counterfactual substitution to approximate the influence of latent confounding factors. Beyond static world modeling, our framework continuously evolves, refining these proxy representations across episodes, enabling efficient adaptation to previously unseen environments. Building on this evolving causally-inspired foundation, our world model supports counterfactual reasoning and strengthens generalization across diverse navigation contexts. Extensive evaluations on established VLN-CE benchmarks demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches, delivering superior navigation performance across diverse scenarios. Real-world robot evaluations further validate the practicality of our approach. Code is available in the Supplementary Material.

title: A Riemannian Framework for the Elastic Analysis of the Spatiotemporal Variability in the Shape and Structure of Tree-Like 4D Objects
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: This paper introduces a novel computational framework for modeling and analyzing the spatiotemporal shape variability of tree-like 4D objects, i.e., three-dimensional structures whose shapes deform and evolve over time. Tree-like 3D objects, such as botanical trees and plants, deform and grow at different rates. In this process, they bend and stretch their branches and change their branching structure, making their spatiotemporal registration challenging. We address this problem within a Riemannian framework that represents tree-like 3D objects as points in a tree-shape space endowed with a proper elastic metric that quantifies branch bending, stretching, and topological changes. With this setting, a 4D tree-like object becomes a trajectory in the tree-shape space. Thus, the problem of modeling and analyzing the spatiotemporal variability in tree-like 4D objects reduces to the analysis of trajectories within this tree-shape space. However, performing spatiotemporal registration and subsequently computing geodesics and statistics in the nonlinear tree-shape space is inherently challenging, as these tasks rely on complex nonlinear optimizations. Our core contribution is the mapping of the tree-like 3D objects to the space of the Extended Square Root Velocity Function (ESRVF) (Srivastava et al., 2011) where the complex elastic metric is reduced to the $\mathbb {L}^{2}$L2 metric. By solving spatial registration in the ESRVF space, analyzing tree-like 4D objects can be reformulated as the problem of analyzing elastic trajectories in the ESRVF space. Based on this formulation, we develop a comprehensive framework for analyzing the spatiotemporal dynamics of tree-like objects, including registration and geodesic computation under large deformations and topological differences, statistical summarization through mean trajectories and modes of variation, and the synthesis of new, random tree-like 4D shapes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework on both synthetic 4D botanical tree models and real plant data, illustrating its robustness and practical applicability in capturing complex spatiotemporal shape evolution.

title: Autoregressive Image to 3D Generation via Next Symmetric View Prediction
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: Autoregressive models via next token prediction have emerged as a promising way towards unified models across multiple modalities for general artificial intelligence. Nevertheless, exploiting this idea to achieve single image to 3D generation remains a challenging problem. In this paper, we introduce a new Autoregressive 3D diffusion model (dubbed as AR3D), that novelly frames autoregressive modeling on multi-view images of 3D content as "next symmetric view prediction." This methodology first triggers 3D autoregressive modeling by remoulding video diffusion model with unidirectional next-view prediction, where the next-view images are iteratively generated conditioned on the past views and input image. Furthermore, a unique autoregressive scheme via next symmetric view prediction is introduced to simultaneously predict each pair of views under the view-order symmetry at each autoregressive step. Such design captures the view-order symmetry of 360$^{\circ }$∘ orbital multi-view images and thus encourages strong geometric and appearance consistency among adjacent views in a near-to-far order. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed AR3D achieves strong performance on both novel view synthesis and single view reconstruction tasks for image-to-3D generation.

title: ShapeLib: Designing a library of programmatic 3D shape abstractions with Large Language Models
abstract: We present ShapeLib , the first method that uses the priors of Large Language Models (LLMs) to design libraries of programmatic 3D shape abstractions. Our system accepts two forms of user-provided design intent: high-level text descriptions of functions to include in the output library and a small seed set of exemplar shapes. We discover a library of abstractions that matches this design intent with a guided LLM workflow that first proposes different ways of applying and implementing functions, and then validates these functions are helpful in representing seed set shapes. To extend beyond the seed set, we develop library-specific recognition networks that map shapes (represented as primitives, voxels, or point clouds) to programs that use these newly discovered abstractions. Across multiple modeling domains (split by shape category), we find that LLMs, when thoughtfully combined with geometric reasoning, can be guided to author libraries of abstraction functions that generalize across shape distributions. Our framework takes a step towards realizing the long-standing shape analysis aspiration of discovering reusable, programmatic shape abstractions while exposing interpretable, semantically aligned interfaces. Our extensive evaluation demonstrates that ShapeLib provides distinct advantages over prior alternative abstraction discovery works in terms of generalization, usability, and maintaining plausibility under manipulation. Finally, we demonstrate that ShapeLib’s abstraction functions unlock a number of downstream applications, combining LLM reasoning over shape programs with geometry processing tools to support shape editing and generation workflows.

title: SPD Matrix Learning for Neuroimaging Analysis: Perspectives, Methods, and Challenges
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: Neuroimaging provides essential tools for characterizing brain activity and inter-regional connectivity through modalities that capture complementary aspects of brain organization. At the same time, extracting meaningful neural signatures remains challenging because each modality introduces its own sources of variability, including measurement noise, spatial and temporal distortions, heterogeneous acquisition protocols, and limited sample sizes. A unifying perspective arises when these data are represented by symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices, such as covariance, connectivity, diffusion, or deformation tensors, which encode second-order statistical relationships or local anatomical structure depending on the modality. Equipping the SPD space with Riemannian geometry yields a non-Euclidean framework for principled statistical analysis and machine learning on these representations. This review organizes learning methodologies on SPD manifolds under a unified framework termed SPD matrix learning. From this perspective, SPD modeling provides a common language across neuroimaging modalities and links modern learning pipelines to decades of geometric statistics.
